title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
This page states and begins Problem I of E526: a naturally straight, uniform, homogeneous elastic rod EF vibrating in any way; find the equation that contains all its possible small motions. Euler specializes the general dynamic elastica equations of the previous page to this case.

(1) Units. The rod has length EF = a and cross-section ('crassities') cc, so its volume is acc. All masses and forces are measured by volumes of the rod's own material. A force b^3 means the weight of a volume b^3 of that substance.

(2) Mass and kinematics. Take arc EX = s. For infinitesimal vibrations s may be identified with the abscissa x. The element ds then has mass cc ds, so the linear density S of the general theory equals cc.

(3) Transverse motion only. At time t the point X has moved to Y, with deflection XY = y small compared with x. Each point can therefore move only along the ordinate, which gives (d^2x/dt^2) = 0, and also ddx = 0 in the spatial differentiation.

(4) Curvature. The general curvature (dy ddx - dx ddy)/ds^3 reduces to -dx ddy/ds^3. The radius of curvature is therefore r = ds^3/(-dx ddy) = -ds^2/ddy, using dx = ds; in modern terms 1/r ≈ -y''. Natural straightness gives ϱ = ∞, so the term V/ϱ drops out.

(5) Stiffness scaling. For geometrically similar rods the 'absolute elasticity' (flexural rigidity) V is taken proportional to the square of the cross-sectional area, V ∝ c^4. Euler writes V = b c^4, with b a material constant.

(6) Dimension of b (continued on the next page). V/r is a moment, i.e. force × length = volume × length = L^4, so V has dimension L^5 and b is a length. In modern terms b c^4 corresponds to EI/(ρg). For a square section I = c^4/12, so b = E/(12ρg): a 'modulus height' depending only on the material.

The page serves to reduce the general equation to the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation. On the next page this becomes (cc/2g) y_tt = -b c^4 y'''' after differentiating.
errors: No substantive error on this page. The identification s = x, the vanishing of d^2x/dt^2 and the curvature formula are all correct to first order.

Notational inconsistency: the radius of curvature is written ϱ on the previous page and r (in V/r) here. ϱ = ∞ refers to the natural (undeformed) radius, r to the current one. This is not an error, but it could confuse a reader.
V ∝ (area)^2 = c^4 holds only for geometrically similar cross-sections, which Euler explicitly assumes ('pro similibus virgis').

ideas.what: Measuring forces and masses by volumes (weights) of the body's own material, with 2g (g = fall height in one second) converting weight to mass
ideas.modern_name: Gravitational units / nondimensionalization by specific weight
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler's standard practice in his mechanics papers
ideas.where_published: Common throughout Euler's mechanics, e.g. E481 and E508 on columns

ideas.what: Small-vibration linearization: arc equals abscissa, purely transverse motion, curvature ≈ -y''
ideas.where_published: Euler, Methodus inveniendi (1744) additamentum on elastic curves; E40; earlier vibration papers

ideas.what: Flexural rigidity V = b c^4 with V ∝ (cross-sectional area)^2 for similar rods; b a material length
ideas.modern_name: Bending stiffness EI with I ∝ A^2; the material constant anticipates Young's modulus expressed as a 'height of the modulus'
ideas.usually_credited_to: Thomas Young (1807) for the modulus as a height; Euler's c^4 rule and length-valued constant are noted by Truesdell
ideas.where_published: Euler's column papers, e.g. E508 'Determinatio onerum quae columnae gestare valent' (1778); discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera Omnia II.11.2)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard specialization of the dynamic elastica to the linear beam equation. The one notable feature, a material constant b with the dimension of length (a precursor of Young's modulus height), also appears in Euler's contemporaneous column papers. Truesdell already discusses it, so nothing here appears missing from the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially faithful to the image.
'idem punctum $x$' appears in italic in the print and is kept as printed; it presumably means the point X.
The page-signature line reads 'O 2' followed by the catchword 'virium'.
